attributes.residual: THREE components, measured. (1) FRAME SLOTS, the part the multiset cannot see: two same-opcode rows carry different displacements -- retail `stw r29,80(r1)` at +0x370 against our `stw r0,108(r1)` at +0x36c, and retail `stw r29,104(r1)` at +0x378 against our `stw r29,80(r1)` at +0x374. Retail's pair of homes is 80/104, ours is 108/80. This is the declaration-order lever and it is the one thing here that is plainly source-shaped. (2) FP SCHEDULE WINDOW in `case 2:` (source lines 1386-1389), reading 0x148:0x1b0: both streams contain exactly the same opcodes but retail issues BOTH integer loads of piece[7] and piece[8] before converting either (`lwz r4,28(r30)` then `lwz r0,32(r30)`, then both `xoris`), while ours interleaves load, convert, load, convert; the dependent `fsubs`/`lfd`/`fmadds` then slide by one slot each. Four int-to-float conversions are present on BOTH sides, which rules out the obvious cure: hoisting `(f32)x` and `(f32)y` into named f32 locals would leave only two conversions and change the instruction count, so retail genuinely converts twice per variable and the source must keep doing so. (3) NAMING, not value: at +0x164/+0x168 retail loads the int-to-float bias constant as `lfd f4,0(0) @lbl_80347400(EMB_SDA21)` while our object names its own anonymous copy `@@308(EMB_SDA21)`. Both are the compiler's own conversion constant and both resolve to the same linked bytes, so this is a pool-NAMING row rather than a wrong constant -- but it is one of the rows inside the 92 and it will not close from statement-level source work. NEXT LANE: run slotdiff.py first per the screened law, attack component (1) by declaration order, and re-read (2) only afterwards -- the FP window is one slot wide and is alignment-sensitive, so its sign may change once the frame homes match.
